Juvenile Indian oil sardines Sardinella longiceps typically recruit to coastal fishing grounds at a modest body size, with published growth curves indicating that the yolk-sac larva stage is extremely abbreviated under typical sea surface temperatures. Field observations confirm that the embryonic period is very brief, with the newly hatched prolarva emerging after only about 2 days [ab = about 2 days] when ambient water temperatures reach 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. At this point of chorion rupture, the emergent yolk-sac larva carries an endogenous nutritive reserve that sustains it until mouth opening and the onset of exogenous feeding. The wet weight at birth for this species is remarkably low, measured at 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value consistent with the minute size of the pelagic egg from which it hatches. This initial mass, derived from an egg diameter in the range of 1 to 4 millimetres, constrains the early larval trajectory and dictates a high reliance on the yolk reserve prior to the critical trophic switch.

Adult Indian oil sardines exhibit a relatively compressed body size compared to many other clupeids, with the species reaching an ultimate total length of 23 centimetres [Li = 23 centimetres] — a size that reflects the fast-growth strategy typical of small pelagic clupeids in productive upwelling ecosystems. This maximum size is attained after several years of steady somatic growth, during which the fish progress through the pelagic larval phase and into the juvenile fingerling stage. Growth rates in natural populations are influenced by seasonal productivity pulses along the western Indian coast, where upwelling drives dense phytoplankton blooms. Corresponding to this modest length, the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 200 grams [Wwi = approximately 200 grams], a mass that represents the upper asymptote of the species' growth trajectory. This body mass is typically achieved after the fish have recruited to the adult spawning stock and have commenced gonadal recrudescence, supporting a robust annual reproductive effort.

The onset of reproductive maturity in Sardinella longiceps is tied to a specific length threshold that is attained during the sub-adult phase, marking the transition into the reproductively viable adult population. Field surveys indicate that the total length at puberty is 16.3 centimetres [Lp = 16.3 centimetres], a size that individuals typically reach within their first year of life under favourable growth conditions — a length that approximates 20 % of maximum body size and aligns with the maturation pattern of many tropical clupeids. At this length, gametogenesis is initiated and the fish become capable of participating in the annual spawning aggregations that characterise the species. This size-based metric provides a reliable predictor of first spawning potential and is used by fisheries managers to estimate the fraction of the stock that is sexually mature. Reaching 16.3 centimetres total length effectively marks the completion of the juvenile growth phase and the entry into the adult component of the population.

At the rearing temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], which is typical of the tropical surface waters inhabited by this species, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 3 years [am = approximately 3 years]. This relatively short life cycle is characteristic of small, fast-growing clupeiform fishes that experience high natural mortality. Longevity records derived from otolith readings and length-frequency analysis confirm that very few individuals survive beyond this age, with senescence and post-reproductive mortality becoming evident during the third year. The age at first reproduction under these same thermal conditions occurs at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching], meaning that the vast majority of spawning takes place in the second year of life at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This timing ensures that most fish have a full breeding season before reaching the terminal stages of their lifespan.

Reproductive output in this species is highly seasonal, with the peak of the spawning event coinciding with the southwest monsoon. At 25 °C [T = 25 °C], individual females perform a single spawning event per year [F_R_i = single spawning event per year], releasing a large batch of pelagic eggs. The maximum reproductive rate under these conditions has been estimated at approximately 257 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 257 eggs per day], a value derived from the species' highest recorded fecundity at optimal thermal regimes. The fertilised ova are broadcast into the water column, where they undergo embryonation and chorionate development before the brief incubation period concludes with eclosion.
